pages.title: AWS Quick Desktop: The Complete Guide (2026) | Balram R.
pages.description: How AWS Quick on desktop works, what it can reach on your machine, and how I set up agents, skills, routines and connectors. Checked against AWS docs.
pages.heading: AWS Quick on desktop: the complete guide
pages.html:
AWS Quick on desktop is the Mac and Windows app for AWS Quick (formerly Amazon Quick). It's an AI assistant for work that can read the folders you choose, drive your browser, run code in a sandbox, and keep agents running on a schedule after you close the lid. I teach AI to a lot of people, and this is the guide I'd hand anyone starting with it: what the app is, how the pieces fit, and the setups I'd copy first.

If you only have ten minutes, read Your first hour and the building blocks table. Everything else goes deeper in eight chapters.

What AWS Quick on desktop is

AWS Quick is AWS's AI workspace for work: chat, research, agents, automations, apps and dashboards in one place. The desktop app is one way into it. The others are the web app, the mobile app and browser or Microsoft 365 extensions. They all share one account, so a chat I start on my laptop is there on my phone.

What the desktop app adds is reach into my machine. It can:

  • read, write, search and index folders I grant, and nothing outside them
  • drive a browser, either a separate copy of my profile or my own running browser
  • run Python or JavaScript in a sandbox to analyse files and build charts
  • use MCP servers I run locally, plus coding agents like Kiro or Claude Code

About the name. The desktop app was announced in preview in April 2026 and became generally available on macOS and Windows in September 2026, as Amazon Quick. In November 2026 the service was renamed AWS Quick. Nothing changed in how it works, and older posts, videos and even the installer file name (Amazon-Quick.dmg) still say Amazon Quick. If you're searching, try both names.

Desktop, web and mobile: what lives where

This is the single idea that clears up most confusion. Quick runs in the cloud. Your history, memory, knowledge graph and anything agents produce are kept in your AWS Quick account. The desktop app is a very capable window plus a set of hands on your computer.

Kept in your AWS Quick account (same on web, mobile and desktop) Only on the desktop app
Conversations and folders of chats Access to the folders you grant
Memory and the knowledge graph Browser automation in your browser
Files agents produce (Agent Files, artifacts) Local code execution in a sandbox
The search index of content you choose to upload Local MCP servers
Agents, skills, Spaces, routines Coding agents (Kiro, Claude Code)
Cloud connectors (Outlook, Slack, Jira and others) The settings for all of the above, plus your sign-in

Two consequences I plan around:

  1. Routines keep running when my laptop is off, because they run in the cloud. A run that needs my machine (a local file, the browser or local code) is different: if my computer is asleep at that moment, the run is skipped and Mission Control says so.
  2. A local MCP server is mine alone. If my team needs the same tools on web and mobile too, it has to be added as a cloud connector.

A tour of the window

What each area is for, in one line:

  • Chat is where you'll spend most of your time. The composer is where you pick the agent, the mode and the thinking effort, attach files, folders or a Space, turn on web search, and type / for commands.
  • Feed is a ranked list of what needs you across email, calendar and messaging, with Calendar and To-dos tabs. It shrinks as you clear it.
  • Library holds everything you and Quick have made: documents, decks, sheets, apps, agents, skills, research.
  • Customize is the workshop: Agents, Skills, Connectors, Knowledge (your folders) and Brand assets.
  • Apps are small interactive tools you build by describing them.
  • Spaces are curated shelves of team content you can chat against.
  • Mission Control (top bar) is the one place to watch every agent, unblock the ones waiting on you, and manage routines.
  • My context (from your profile) shows what Quick has learned: Memories and the Knowledge graph.

Three controls I'd learn on day one: /goal (give it a job to finish, and it keeps working and checks itself before handing back), Cmd+B / Ctrl+B (push the running task into the background and carry on in another chat), and Incognito (a chat that doesn't read or write memory and isn't saved; switch it on before the first message, because you can't once the chat has started).

Your first hour

Here's the order I'd follow. Each step takes about ten minutes.

  1. Install and sign in. Apple Silicon Mac (macOS 12 or later) or 64-bit Windows 10 or later, 8 GB RAM. Use the work sign-in your admin gave you, or a personal sign-in for the Free plan. Chapter 1, coming soon, will cover the first-launch security prompts.
  2. Connect three things only: calendar, email and one messaging app. The first-run screen offers exactly these. Skip the rest for now.
  3. Grant one folder, not your whole drive. Pick a project folder. Leave indexing off until you know what you want searchable from your phone. Chapter 6, coming soon, will explain what each indexing switch uploads.
  4. Ask three real questions about today: "What do I need to prepare for my meetings today?", "What did I miss in [channel] since Friday?", "Summarise the files in [folder] and list open decisions." Check the citations on each answer.
  5. Save one skill. Finish a small multi-step task in chat (a status update is perfect) and accept the offer to save the steps as a skill, or ask it to. Chapter 4 has a ready-made one.
  6. Put one agent on a routine. A morning meeting-prep agent on weekdays is the easiest win. Chapter 3 has the full build.

At the end of the hour you've seen the three things that make the desktop app worth installing: it knows your day, it can use your files, and it keeps working when you don't.

The building blocks: chat, skill, agent, routine, Space, App

People mix these up constantly, and the wrong choice makes the right result much harder. Here's how I decide.

You want... Use Why
An answer or a draft, once Chat Nothing to set up. Use /goal if it's a job, not a question.
The same task done the same way every time, by anyone Skill A skill is a written method. Any agent can pick it up when the task comes up.
A specialist with its own instructions, sources, tools and memory Agent An agent is who does the work and what it's allowed to touch.
Work to happen without you asking Routine A routine is a schedule that wakes an agent with instructions. It runs in the cloud.
Answers grounded only in an agreed set of documents Space While attached, Quick answers from the Space and tells you when the answer isn't there.
A reusable interactive tool for other people App For a form, a calculator or a dashboard people click, not chat with.

My rule of thumb: start in chat, turn the method into a skill, give it to an agent when it needs its own tools or memory, and add a routine only after a manual run works. Most people jump straight to an agent with a routine and then can't tell which part went wrong.

Two other guides on this site go deeper on single pieces: the AWS Quick Flows guide builds a scheduled weekly report step by step, and Combining AWS Quick, Kiro, MCP and SKILL.md covers when you need a connector and when a skill is enough.

Modes, thinking effort and agent hours

Every chat and every routine runs on one of three modes, plus a thinking effort:

  • Fast for lookups and simple tasks. No extended thinking.
  • Balanced for most work: writing, summaries, everyday analysis.
  • Smart for hard analysis and anything where accuracy matters most.
  • Thinking effort (Off, Low, Medium, High) is a separate dial on Balanced and Smart.

Usage is measured in agent hours: time Quick spends actively working, metered per second, at a higher rate in heavier modes and higher thinking levels. Idle time between your messages doesn't count. A routine uses hours every time it runs, so ten small routines add up. Plans and allowances change, so check the AWS Quick pricing page rather than any number in a blog post, including this one. On the check date, the Free plan includes the desktop app.

From my desk. I run a heavy custom agent with a long, detailed set of instructions. On Fast it ran out of context partway through, and on Smart it got throttled at busy times. Balanced was the mode that finished reliably. If a big agent keeps failing, try Balanced before you rewrite the prompt.

How it compares with other desktop AI apps

All of these products ship changes every month, so treat this as a snapshot on the check date and follow the links.

The difference that matters most in practice is what happens to scheduled work when you shut the laptop:

App Scheduled work while your computer is off
AWS Quick on desktop Routines run in the cloud. A run that needs your machine (local files, the browser, local code) is skipped if it's off.
Claude desktop Cloud scheduled tasks keep running. Local scheduled tasks only fire while the app is open and the computer is awake.

Where Quick stands out for me is that it isn't tied to one vendor's suite: the same assistant reads Outlook or Gmail, Slack or Teams, Jira or Asana, and your local folders, and routines keep going after the laptop closes. If your whole company lives in one suite and you only need help inside it, that suite's own assistant may be the simpler choice.

Limits worth knowing

The ones people hit first, on the check date: 3 chat sessions running at once, 20 scheduled tasks per user with at least 15 minutes between runs, 50 MB per attached file, 50,000 characters of agent instructions, and approvals that expire after 12 hours. The full, dated table will be in Chapter 8, Troubleshooting and limits (coming soon).

Frequently asked questions

Is AWS Quick the same as Amazon Quick?

Yes. Amazon Quick was renamed AWS Quick in November 2026. The product, your data and your settings didn't change. Amazon Quick Sight is now AWS Quick Sight.

Is the AWS Quick desktop app free?

There's a Free plan for individuals that includes the desktop app, and paid plans for teams and organisations with more usage. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Does it run on Intel Macs or Linux?

The documented minimum is an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) on macOS 12 or later, or 64-bit Windows 10 or later. Linux isn't listed.

Does it keep working when my laptop is closed?

Routines and the feed do, because they run in the cloud. A run that needs your computer (a local file, the browser, local code) only runs when the computer is on with the app running and connected.

Does AWS use my conversations to train models?

No. AWS's desktop security page says your conversations, files and personal context aren't used for model training. Chapter 6, coming soon, will cover memory, the knowledge graph, Incognito and how to delete things.

Can I connect my own MCP servers?

Yes. On desktop, add a local connector for a server that runs on your computer or at a URL. To share a server across web, mobile and desktop, set it up as a cloud connector. Chapter 5, coming soon, will walk through both.

Can it use Kiro or Claude Code?

Yes, as coding agents. Quick hands the coding task over and reports back. Its own code sandbox blocks common coding commands, so real development goes to the coding agent.

What's the difference between a skill and an agent?

A skill is a method (how to do a task). An agent is a worker (instructions, sources, tools and its own memory). Agents use skills.

Sources

  • What is AWS Quick on desktop?
  • Understanding the desktop interface
  • Working with chat
  • AWS Quick desktop usage limits
  • AWS Quick pricing
  • Amazon Quick is now AWS Quick
  • Amazon Quick desktop app is now generally available on macOS and Windows
  • Comparison sources: Claude Code Desktop scheduled tasks, Local MCP servers on Claude Desktop

pages.title: AWS Quick Agents, Routines & Mission Control | Balram R.
pages.description: Build an AWS Quick agent, put it on a routine that runs while your laptop is off, and manage every run from Mission Control. Copyable setups inside.
pages.heading: Agents, routines and Mission Control in AWS Quick
pages.html:
This is the chapter where AWS Quick on desktop stops being a chat window and starts doing work while you're elsewhere. I'll cover what an agent is, how to build one that behaves, how routines run (and when they quietly don't), and how to use Mission Control to keep a handful of agents honest. Two full builds are at the end, ready to copy.

What an agent is

An agent is a version of Quick with a job description. You give it instructions, the sources it may read, the tools it may use, and it keeps its own memory of how you like that job done. Quick itself is the built-in agent you talk to by default; everything you build sits next to it.

Two rules shape everything else:

  • An agent can only reach what you can reach. It acts with your access, through the connectors and folders you've allowed, and within the tool permissions you've set (Chapter 5, coming soon).
  • Each agent learns separately. A preference you teach your meeting-prep agent doesn't leak into your writing agent. The knowledge graph of people and projects is shared, though, so every agent knows who "Priya from finance" is.

Build your first agent

The fastest path is to describe it. In any chat, type something like "I want to create an agent that prepares me for meetings", or go to Customize > Agents > Create > From chat. Quick drafts a name, a description and instructions, and you refine them by talking or by editing the fields.

From file imports an agent definition that was exported to JSON, which is handy for moving a tested agent between accounts.

What to do in the first ten minutes:

  1. Let Quick draft it, then rewrite the instructions yourself as plain steps. Short and specific beats long and general.
  2. Attach one or two reference documents if the agent needs house style or a template.
  3. Turn on only the capabilities it needs. Web search off unless the job needs the open web.
  4. Test it in chat with three real requests, including one that should fail politely.
  5. Only then publish.

You can also @-mention an agent in any chat to use it inline, which opens its editor in a session tab if you want to tweak it on the spot.

What's inside an agent

The editor has two tabs.

Instructions

  • Name and Description. The description is what people see when they browse shared agents, so write it for them.
  • Instructions. Up to 50,000 characters with headings, lists and code. You'll rarely need a tenth of that.
  • Welcome message with starter prompts, so someone opening the agent knows what to ask.

Capabilities

  • Web search on or off.
  • Skills. By default an agent can use every skill you have. Add specific skills and it's limited to those. Limiting the skills of an agent other people will use keeps it behaving the same for everyone.
  • Spaces. The shared content the agent reads from.
  • Connections. The connectors and tools it may use.

Each agent also gets a landing page with four tabs: Overview (what needs your input, plus an AI-written briefing of its recent work), Activities (filter by All, Needs input, Running, Routines), Agent Files (everything it has produced across runs) and Settings.

A run shows Running while it works and Needs input when it's waiting on you. When it ends it's Completed, Interrupted or Failed. The Agents list summarises the last run, for example "Last run failed", which is the first column worth scanning each morning.

Draft, publish and share

Agents are versioned, and this trips people up:

  • You edit a draft. Your changes don't affect anyone, or any routine, until you publish.
  • Routines only ever use the published version. If you fix the instructions and the routine still misbehaves, check that you published.
  • Agents are private until you share them, and you can't share one until it's published. Add release notes when you publish; your team sees them.
  • When you share an agent, share its sources too. People only get answers from sources they can access themselves. You don't have to share everything, just what the agent needs.

The agent's menu lets you set it as the default for new chats, export it to JSON, duplicate it, switch versions, manage its routines, uninstall it (removes it from your list only) or delete it (gone for everyone, if you own it). Published agents can be used from Quick on the web as well.

Routines: agents on a schedule

A routine wakes an agent at a set time with a set of instructions. Today the routine type on desktop is a schedule, for example "every weekday at 8:30 AM".

Create one in three ways: Mission Control > Create, the Routines tab on an agent's page, or just ask in chat: "every morning at 9, check my channels and summarise what I missed".

The routine form has two tabs. Overview holds the settings; Activity is the run history.

Field What goes there
Repeats How often and at what time. The shortest gap allowed is 15 minutes.
Custom time range Optional start, end and time zone. Useful for a routine that only matters during a launch.
Triggers The agent to run.
Uses The connectors and tools this routine may use. Nothing else is available to it.
Instructions What to do on each run. Write it as if the agent has no memory of yesterday.
Model details Model (Fast, Balanced, Smart), thinking effort, whether to include memory, and whether it may split work into parallel sub-tasks.

The behaviour to understand is in that diagram. Routines run in the cloud, so a morning brief built on email, calendar and messaging arrives even if your laptop is in a bag. A run that needs your machine (reading a local file, the browser or local code) only works if the computer is on with the app running and connected. Otherwise that run is skipped. If a routine needs a local file every day, either move the file into a Space or accept that it only runs on days you're at your desk.

Two more things to plan for:

  • Approvals pause the run. If the routine wants to send an email and the tool is set to Ask each time, it waits. An approval you've given stays valid for 12 hours before Quick asks again.
  • Every run costs agent hours. A routine every 15 minutes in Smart mode adds up fast. Start daily, in Balanced, and only tighten the schedule if the result earns it.

Quick also ships with built-in routines, such as the feed agent that fills your activity feed. You can change their schedule, tools, instructions and model like any other routine.

Mission Control

Mission Control is the control room for all your agents. Click its icon in the top bar for a quick popover (runs, items waiting on you, routines), or open the full page.

What it's best for, roughly in order of how often you'll need it:

  1. Unblocking. Filter to agents that need input and approve, deny or reply in chat with a clarification.
  2. Checking last night's runs. Open a finished run to see what it did, the files it made, a longer summary and the events of each sub-task, then chat to follow up.
  3. Stopping a runaway. On a live run you can watch events as they happen, pause it or cancel it.
  4. Managing routines for every agent in one list, instead of opening each agent.
  5. Usage. The Runs this week tile opens a page with your runs and an Agent hours card showing how much runtime you've used. If you share agents or apps, Creator analytics shows how many people use them (refreshed hourly).

Build 1: a meeting-prep agent

Goal: before each workday, a short brief on every meeting: who's in it, what was said last time, what's open, and one question worth asking.

Before you start: connect your calendar, email and messaging app (Customize > Connectors).

Create the agent with From chat, then replace the instructions with these:

text
You prepare me for my meetings.

For each meeting on my calendar for the day:
1. Title, time and attendees. Mark anyone I haven't met before.
2. Context: the last email thread, chat thread or document that mentions this meeting or its topic in the past 30 days. Cite each one.
3. Open items: decisions or actions from earlier threads that are still open, with the owner if it's clear.
4. One question I should ask, based on the open items.

Rules:
- Skip meetings marked as focus time, personal or declined.
- If you can't find context for a meeting, say "No prior context found" instead of guessing.
- Keep each meeting under 120 words. Plain bullets, no tables.
- Never send, accept or decline anything. This is read-only.

Capabilities: web search off; connections to calendar, email and messaging only.

Test it in chat first: "Prepare me for tomorrow's meetings." Check that every claim has a citation and that a meeting with no history says so.

Then add the routine:

Field Value
Repeats Every weekday at 7:30 AM, your time zone
Triggers Meeting prep
Uses Calendar, email, messaging
Instructions "Prepare my brief for today's meetings and post it to my feed."
Model details Balanced, thinking Low, include memory on, sub-tasks on

Because it only uses cloud connectors, it runs whether your laptop is open or not.

Build 2: a channel-digest routine

Goal: one end-of-day summary of the channels you can't keep up with, sorted by what needs you.

This one doesn't need a custom agent. Point a routine at the built-in Quick agent.

Field Value
Repeats Every weekday at 5:30 PM
Triggers Quick
Uses Your messaging connector only
Model details Fast or Balanced, thinking Off, include memory on

Instructions:

text
Summarise today's activity in these channels: [channel 1], [channel 2], [channel 3].

Group the summary into:
1. Needs me: direct questions to me, mentions, or decisions waiting on my team.
2. Worth knowing: launches, changes in plans, new documents.
3. Skip: everything else, as a single count.

For each item give one line, the channel, and a link to the message.
Don't reply to or react to anything.
If a channel had no activity, say so in one line.

Run it once with the play button before you switch it on, and compare it with what you'd have picked out yourself. If it misses things, tighten "Needs me" with names of people or projects.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Scheduling before testing. Run the agent by hand three times first. A routine just repeats whatever mistake it has.
  • Editing the draft and forgetting to publish. The routine keeps running the old version.
  • A local step in an overnight routine. It gets skipped while your computer sleeps. Use cloud sources for anything that must run every day.
  • Giving every agent every tool. Narrow the Uses list. It's safer and the agent is easier to read.
  • One giant agent. Two small agents with clear jobs beat one that does everything. If it's a method rather than a job, it should be a skill (Chapter 4).

Frequently asked questions

Do AWS Quick routines run when my laptop is closed?

Yes, routines run in the cloud. A run that needs your computer (a local file, the browser or local code) only runs if the computer is on with the app running and connected; otherwise that run is skipped.

How many routines can I have?

On the check date, up to 20 scheduled tasks per user, with at least 15 minutes between runs. Chapter 8, coming soon, will have the full limits table.

Why did my routine ignore my latest changes?

Routines run the published version of an agent. Publish your draft.

Can other people use my agent?

Yes, after you publish and share it. Share the sources it needs too, or they'll get answers only from sources they can already see.

Where do an agent's outputs go?

Into its Agent Files, its Activities tab and Mission Control, and routines send their results to your feed or to a connected app.

Which mode should a routine use?

Start with Balanced. Use Fast for simple summaries and Smart only when accuracy really matters, because heavier modes use more agent hours.

Sources

  • Agents
  • Mission Control
  • Activity feed
  • Memories
  • AWS Quick desktop usage limits
  • Troubleshooting

pages.title: AWS Quick Skills: SKILL.md Guide and Template | Balram R.
pages.description: How AWS Quick skills load, how to write a SKILL.md that triggers at the right time, and a weekly status skill you can copy, test, publish and share.
pages.heading: Skills in AWS Quick: write one, test it, share it
pages.html:
If agents are the workers in AWS Quick, skills are the methods they follow. A good skill means you explain a task once and get it done the same way every time, by you or by anyone you share it with. This chapter covers how Quick decides when to use a skill, how to write one that triggers when it should (and not when it shouldn't), and a weekly status skill you can copy.

What a skill is

Every skill is a folder, and at its top sits a file called SKILL.md. That file holds two things:

  • a description: one or two sentences on what the skill is for and when to use it
  • instructions: the steps to follow, which can be a whole multi-step process

The folder can also carry reference files (templates, examples, scripts) and point to the tools it needs, such as a connector or a built-in capability. The skill names the tools; it doesn't contain them or grant access to them. Access still comes from your connectors and permissions (Chapter 5, coming soon).

If you've used skills in Kiro or Claude Code, the idea is the same. That's useful: a method written once can travel between tools with small edits.

Skill or agent?

The two are easy to mix up.

Compare Skill Agent
What it is A method: how to do one task A worker: who does a job, with what
Holds Description, instructions, reference files, tools it needs Instructions, capabilities, Spaces, connections, its own memory and files
Runs on a schedule Through an agent's routine Yes, with a routine
Who uses it Any agent, including Quick You and anyone you share it with
Good for Status updates, brand-checked posts, report formats, review checklists Meeting prep, inbox triage, a project monitor

My shortcut: if the instructions start with "When you write a...", it's a skill. If they start with "You are responsible for...", it's an agent. And an agent can use skills, so the best setups are usually a small agent plus two or three skills.

A skill is also different from a connector. A connector gives Quick access to a tool; a skill tells it how to do the work once it's there. The MCP and SKILL.md guide on this site covers that split in more depth.

How Quick loads skills

Quick doesn't read every skill into every chat. It works in two stages.

  1. Discovery. Quick looks at the name and description of your enabled skills to decide whether one fits your request.
  2. Activation. When one fits, or when you name it, Quick reads the full instructions into the conversation and follows them, along with the files and tools the skill refers to.

The practical upshot: the description decides whether your skill is ever used. The instructions decide how well. Most skills that "don't work" have a fine method and a vague description.

You can also trigger a skill by name ("use the weekly status skill") or start a chat with it loaded from Try it on its detail panel. Type /skills in chat to see what's available.

What's in a skill folder

text
weekly-status/
├── SKILL.md          the description and the steps
├── template.md       the layout to fill in
└── examples/
    └── good-update.md   one update you liked

Keep it small. The whole skill can be up to 6 MB on the check date, but a skill that needs megabytes of reference material is usually a Space in disguise.

Three ways to create one

Go to Customize > Skills > Create and choose:

  • From chat. Describe the skill and Quick drafts the instructions, picks the tools to reference and writes the SKILL.md. This is where I'd start.
  • From file. Upload a .md or a .zip.
  • From folder. Point at a folder with SKILL.md at the top and its reference files.

The easiest skill of all: complete a task with several steps in chat, and Quick may offer to save the steps as a skill. If it doesn't, ask it to. You then edit a method that has already worked once, instead of writing one from scratch.

Writing a description that triggers

A description has one job: make Quick pick this skill for the right requests and ignore it for the rest. What works:

  • Name the output and the moment. "Writes my weekly status update for my manager" beats "Helps with updates".
  • Use the words people actually type. If people say "weekly report" and "Friday update", put both in.
  • Say when not to use it. "Not for project launch announcements" stops it hijacking nearby requests.
  • Keep it to two sentences. It's a label on a shelf, not the manual.

Build: a weekly status skill

Goal: every Friday, a status update in the same shape, drawn from the week's real activity, in your voice.

SKILL.md

markdown
---
name: weekly-status
display_name: Weekly status
description: Writes my weekly status update (also called the Friday update or weekly report) from this week's email, calendar, messages and documents. Not for launch announcements or customer emails.
icon: "📝"
trigger: weekly status
---

# Weekly status update

Use template.md for the layout. Match the tone of examples/good-update.md.

## Steps
1. Find the reporting week: Monday to today, in my time zone.
2. Gather what I worked on: meetings I attended, threads I replied to, documents I created or edited. Cite each source.
3. Group the work under my current projects. If something doesn't fit a project, put it under "Other".
4. For each project write:
   - Done: finished outcomes, not activity ("Shipped X", not "Worked on X").
   - Next: what happens next week, with an owner.
   - Risks: anything blocked or late, with what would unblock it.
5. Keep the whole update under 250 words.
6. Show me the draft. Never send it.

## Rules
- If you can't find evidence for an item, leave it out rather than guess.
- No adjectives like "great" or "amazing". Facts and numbers only.
- If a project had no activity this week, write "No update" for it.

Put the two files and an examples/ folder with one update you liked into a folder, then use Create > From folder. Or paste the instructions into From chat and let Quick build the files.

Getting the header right

The block between the two --- lines is the skill's header, and AWS's official skill catalog on GitHub documents the fields: name (lower-case with hyphens, the same as the folder name), display_name, description, icon (one emoji), trigger (a short phrase that activates it) and tools (leave this out rather than guess tool names). Three things break it quietly, with no error message:

  • Anything above the first ---, even a blank line. Quick then finds no header at all.
  • Several keys on one line. One key per line, starting at the left edge.
  • A # in front of a key. That turns the line into a comment.

When it goes wrong, the skill installs with a blank name and the whole header shows up as text in its instructions. And if you build a skill in the Create form instead, the header fields are the form's own boxes: paste only the part below the closing --- into Instructions.

Test, publish and share

A skill you own has a draft and a published version. Edits go to the draft and show an Unpublished changes label; the published version keeps running unchanged until you publish. That means you can improve a skill people rely on without breaking it halfway.

A test routine worth running before every publish:

  1. Try it with a normal request: "Write my weekly status."
  2. Try it with a request phrased differently: "Can you do my Friday update?" If it doesn't trigger, fix the description.
  3. Try it with something it should ignore: "Draft a launch announcement." If it triggers, add a "Not for..." line.
  4. Check that every item in the output is backed by a real source.

Then:

  • Publish makes the draft live. Everyone who has the skill moves to the new version.
  • Share is a separate step. Pick people or groups, or the whole account with Share with all. Publishing alone shares nothing.

People you share with find it under Shared with me in Add to Quick. They're viewers: they can use it, and their copy tracks your published version, but they can't edit or re-share it. To change it, they Duplicate it into a copy they own. Only you, as the owner, can change, publish, share, export or delete it. Careful with Delete: it removes the skill for everyone you shared it with, not just you.

System and official skills

Quick comes with system skills marked with a System badge, for documents, presentations, spreadsheets, web browsing, code execution, the knowledge graph and transcription. You can try them and switch them off, but not edit or share them. When you ask for a deck, the presentations skill loads on its own.

On the Skills tab, Browse all lists Official skills from AWS Quick (everyday productivity, skills for roles like Sales, Marketing and Legal, and sets for specific industries) and skills shared within your organisation. Adding one links you to the owner's live version rather than copying it, so you get their updates automatically.

Before writing a skill from scratch, check the Official list. Duplicating a close match and editing it is faster.

Admin controls

In a company account, admins can narrow what you can do with skills through custom permissions: turn skills off entirely, block sharing with individuals, block sharing with the whole account, or make every share wait for approval. If Share is greyed out, that's usually why. Chapter 7, coming soon, will cover the admin side.

Frequently asked questions

What is a SKILL.md file in AWS Quick?

It's the file at the top of a skill folder. It holds the skill's description, which Quick uses to decide when the skill applies, and the instructions it follows when the skill is active.

Why isn't my skill being used?

Usually the description. Quick picks skills by name and description first, so describe the output, the moment and the words people actually use. Also check the skill is enabled, and that the agent you're using isn't limited to a different set of skills.

Does publishing a skill share it?

No. Publishing makes your draft the live version. Sharing is a separate step where you choose who gets it.

Can I edit a skill someone shared with me?

Not directly. Duplicate it to get your own copy, then edit that.

Can I use the same skill in Kiro or Claude Code?

The idea and the file name are the same, so a method usually moves across with small edits. Tool references and paths will differ between products, so test it in each one.

How big can a skill be?

On the check date, up to 6 MB per skill and up to 1,000 skills per user. Chapter 8, coming soon, will have the full limits table.
